items.title: Cutting an integral into 100 trapezoids beats analytical integration for most real problems
items.claim: Most integrals appearing in physics, engineering or statistics do NOT have closed-form solutions. They're computed numerically. The simplest method (trapezoidal rule) divides the interval into strips and approximates each as a trapezoid.

options.text: Error in the trapezoidal rule is O(1/n^2) where n is the number of strips. Simpson's rule (quadratic interpolation) is O(1/n^4). Gauss-Legendre and adaptive quadrature can achieve essentially machine precision for well-behaved integrands
Always less accurate than analytical answers

items.reveal:
Trapezoidal rule: approximate integral from a to b of f(x) dx by the sum of trapezoidal strips. Error scales as h^2 (where h is the strip width), so halving h quarters the error.

Simpson's rule (uses quadratic fits to triples of points): error scales as h^4. Halving h reduces error by 16x.

For a function smooth enough on [a, b], Simpson's rule with 20 strips can give 6-7 decimal places of accuracy. Gauss-Legendre quadrature with 10 nodes can give 10-15 decimal places.

Many real-world integrals:
- integral of e^(-x^2) dx: no elementary antiderivative. Used everywhere in statistics. Always computed numerically (or via the error function erf).
- integral of sin(x)/x dx: no elementary form. Defined as the sine integral Si(x).
- integral over irregular domains, multidimensional integrals, integrals with singularities — numerical methods are standard.

Monte Carlo integration: for high-dimensional integrals (d > ~4), grid-based methods (Simpson, Gauss) suffer the 'curse of dimensionality' — n grid points per axis means n^d total. Monte Carlo (random sampling) has error O(1/sqrt(N)) independent of dimension; the standard tool for integrals in 10+ dimensions (e.g., statistical mechanics, finance).

More sophisticated: adaptive quadrature (refines where the function is wiggly), Romberg's method, Chebyshev quadrature for analytic functions, sparse grids, quasi-Monte Carlo with low-discrepancy sequences (Sobol, Halton).

The trade-off between numerical and analytical: analytical is exact when available, but unavailable for most functions. Numerical is universally applicable, with accuracy dialed up by computational cost.
items.why: Calculus class focuses on analytical integration. Real applied math is largely numerical — and the numerical methods can be vastly faster and more accurate than the analytical ones for the integrals actually needed.

items.title: A university that favoured women overall was sued for discriminating against them
items.claim: Berkeley's graduate admissions, 1973: men admitted at 44%, women at 35%. Looks like discrimination. Break it down by department — and in most departments, women were admitted at HIGHER rates. The overall trend reverses when disaggregated.
items.prompt: How can the parts and the whole point opposite ways?

options.text: Simpson's paradox: women applied disproportionately to highly competitive departments with low admission rates for everyone; the overall ratio is dominated by where applicants applied, not how each department treated them
Only one of the figures is true

items.reveal_title: Simpson's paradox in real admissions data
items.reveal:
Bickel, Hammel and O'Connell (Science 1975) analysed Berkeley's 1973 fall admissions. Aggregate: 44% of male applicants admitted vs 35% of female. Looks like a 9-point bias.

Department-by-department: of the 6 largest departments, 4 actually favoured women (higher admission rate). Only 2 favoured men.

What's going on: women disproportionately applied to humanities and social sciences (low admission rates for everyone, ~5-30%). Men disproportionately applied to physics, engineering, etc. (higher admission rates, ~50-70%). The aggregate bias against women was driven by their CHOICE of department, not by departmental policies.

The pattern is named after Edward H. Simpson (1951 statistician), though Pearson and Yule had noted it earlier.

The lesson: aggregating data across groups can REVERSE the direction of a trend present in every group. Whenever you see a aggregate correlation in observational data, ask whether breaking it down by relevant subgroup changes the story.

Real-world examples: kidney stone treatment effectiveness, racial sentencing disparities, COVID death rates by age, batting averages across seasons.
items.why: Aggregate statistics feel definitive. Disaggregating by a confounder can reverse the apparent trend — sometimes drastically. The same data tell different stories at different levels.

items.title: The chain rule explains why a car's acceleration depends on both gear and rpm
items.claim: A car's speed (v) depends on engine rpm (omega) through the gear ratio. Engine rpm depends on time as the driver presses the throttle. The chain rule says dv/dt = (dv/d(omega)) * (d(omega)/dt). Acceleration is the product of two derivatives.
items.prompt: What's the chain rule's geometric meaning?

options.text: When y depends on u and u depends on t, a small change in t produces a small change in u (scaled by du/dt) which produces a small change in y (scaled by dy/du); chaining the scalings gives dy/dt = (dy/du)(du/dt)
It is wrong for vector quantities

items.reveal_title: The chain rule as composition of rates
items.reveal:
If y = f(u) and u = g(t), then y = f(g(t)). The chain rule: dy/dt = f'(g(t)) * g'(t) = (dy/du) * (du/dt).

Geometric intuition: a small Delta t produces a small Delta u (approximately (du/dt) * Delta t), which produces a small Delta y (approximately (dy/du) * Delta u). Combining: Delta y ≈ (dy/du)(du/dt) Delta t. Take the limit and you get the chain rule.

Physics examples:
- A particle's position depends on time. Its velocity depends on its position (e.g., in a velocity field). Acceleration = (dv/dx)(dx/dt) = v dv/dx. This is the Eulerian-Lagrangian connection in fluid mechanics.
- Optics: refractive index varies with position. The ray equation involves chain rules through the index.
- Thermodynamics: pressure depends on temperature and volume. Derivatives form a web of chain rules — Maxwell relations.

The chain rule is the BACKBONE of backpropagation in neural networks: gradients of a loss with respect to weights are computed via chain rules through layers of the network. Training deep neural networks is essentially repeated chain rule applications across millions of parameters.

When u or g has multiple components (vector-valued), the chain rule becomes the JACOBIAN rule — products of matrices of partial derivatives.
items.why: The chain rule looks like a notational identity. It's the fundamental principle of compositional change — appearing in physics, optimisation, neural networks, and any setting where one variable depends on another through an intermediate.
